questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: state the three classic functions of a political party
questions.stem: A political party is said to perform three classic functions in a democracy. Which set of three matches that standard account?

options.text: Nominating candidates for office, shaping policy, and mobilising voters
Nominating candidates, legislating directly, and hearing court cases
options.misconception: believes a party itself exercises the legislative and judicial powers of the state

options.text: Recruiting civil servants, setting tax rates, and fixing the term of office
options.misconception: confuses party organisation with the bureaucracy and the legislature

options.text: Supervising vote counts, accrediting broadcasters, and drafting statutes
options.misconception: thinks a party polices the neutral institutions that must judge elections

questions.explanation: The standard account gives a party three jobs. It supplies candidates so that voters have a choice of people, it puts competing programmes in front of the electorate so that policy alternatives exist at all, and it mobilises and informs voters so that attachment and turnout survive between elections. None of that gives a party the power to legislate, tax, judge or certify a ballot, because those powers sit with separate institutions that a party must win at an election. The trap is to fold the functions of the state into the functions of the party.
questions.hint: Ask which three things a party does without ever holding public office.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a party system from a list of registered parties
questions.stem: Two countries keep registers that name the same thirty political parties, yet in one many of those parties can win seats while in two only ever win. What best explains the difference?

options.text: Only the second constrains competition enough that most registered parties cannot win
The first requires more registration paperwork from each party than the second
options.misconception: believes the number of registered parties is what makes a party system competitive

options.text: The second bans the smaller parties from naming a candidate in any district
options.misconception: invents a ban on candidate nomination to explain a seat outcome

options.text: The first gives every constituency a much larger electorate than the second does
options.misconception: attributes party viability to electorate size rather than to barriers to entry

questions.explanation: A party system is the effective pattern of competition among parties, not the list of names on a register. Its dimensions are how many parties are relevant, how easily a newcomer can enter, and how intense the competition is. Registering a label proves only that the name exists; if thresholds, financing rules or district magnitude stop that party converting votes into seats, it is not part of the pattern that matters. Electorate size shapes how seats are allocated, but it does not decide how many parties can win.
questions.hint: Ask whether the parties on the register can actually convert votes into seats.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: locate where competition occurs in a single-party system
questions.stem: One legal party is guaranteed a legislative majority and no rival can take a seat. Where does the decisive competition for political leadership tend to take place?

options.text: Inside the single party, in contests for its own leadership and positions
Between the party and the commission that supervises how votes are counted
options.misconception: mistakes electoral administration for a contest over political leadership

options.text: Between unregistered civic groups that operate entirely outside the party system
options.misconception: assumes a banned party is replaced by open civic competition for office

options.text: Between the party and a head of state who appoints the prime minister
options.misconception: confuses an office-filling rule with the location of party competition

questions.explanation: If one party holds a legislative majority by arrangement, voters cannot remove it at an election, so the contest that decides who governs shifts to the selection of the party's own leader and the allocation of its internal posts. A single-party system relocates competition rather than abolishing it, which is why the internal struggle can be sharper than any inter-party fight would have been. Counting a ballot is a neutral administrative task, and a ceremonial appointment rule describes something else entirely.
questions.hint: Ask where a challenger can still defeat the current leadership by lawful means.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain why two-party systems pull parties toward the centre
questions.stem: In a two-party system both parties repeatedly narrow the gap between their positions. Which feature of the system produces that movement?

options.text: Each party needs the voters who would otherwise be drawn to its only rival
Every tied constituency is awarded to whichever party is the older body
options.misconception: invents a rule about tied districts to explain a shift in policy

options.text: Both parties are required to publish identical positions on every question
options.misconception: believes convergence means the two parties have adopted one platform

options.text: The party that finishes second is dissolved by law after every election
options.misconception: invents an enforced dissolution that would end competition altogether

questions.explanation: With only two parties, the votes a party can gain are those its opponent already holds, so the voters who could go either way decide both the seat and the party's incentive. Alienating a committed supporter is cheaper than losing that floating group, which pushes each party toward the middle. Neither age of a party nor a rule about ties produces this, and copying the rival on every question would mean the two were competing with each other rather than courting anyone.
questions.hint: Ask whose votes a party stands to gain, given that there is only one alternative.

questions.learningObjective: state the condition under which a coalition government can be formed
questions.stem: A fragmented election leaves no party with a legislative majority and several parties are willing to govern. What has to be true before a cabinet drawn from them can exist at all?

options.text: A combination of the parties has to command a legislative majority
The largest party has to be willing to govern with no partner beside it
options.misconception: believes a cabinet can be formed without any support in the chamber

options.text: The parties must first agree to hold a referendum on the coalition agreement
options.misconception: treats a referendum as a precondition of forming a government

options.text: The returning officer must certify that no single party won a majority
options.misconception: believes an administrative certificate is what authorises a coalition

questions.explanation: A coalition is an agreement to govern together, and it lasts only as long as the arithmetic that produced it. The parties in it must between them be able to command a legislative majority, or the government fails the first time it is tested. If the largest party can govern alone no coalition is required, a referendum has no bearing on forming a government, and the absence of a majority is a fact about the result that creates the need for a coalition rather than a certificate that authorises one.
questions.hint: Ask what happens the first time the new cabinet faces a confidence vote.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: trace the consequence of parties originating outside the state
questions.stem: The first parties were built by organised groups of voters rather than created by the state. Which feature of parties today follows from that origin?

options.text: They remain voluntary associations that must win support to hold office
They take public office as soon as they are registered with the authorities
options.misconception: believes registration confers a right to office rather than a duty to compete

options.text: They are financed entirely by the state because they began as public bodies
options.misconception: treats a voluntary association as an organ of the state

options.text: They may issue rules that bind every citizen on matters of party policy
options.misconception: confuses a party rule with a law binding the whole polity

questions.explanation: Because parties grew out of the franchise rather than out of the state, they entered politics as organisations seeking office and needing votes, not as authorities already in possession of it. That is why a party commands nothing until an election hands it a mandate, and why it loses that mandate when support goes at the next election. Registration is a formality that lets a party compete, and a party rule binds only the members who accepted it.
questions.hint: Ask whether a party could hold office before any voters had backed it.

questions.learningObjective: explain the decline of mass party membership
questions.stem: Formal party membership has fallen steeply in many democracies while elections stay just as competitive. Which change best explains that pattern?

options.text: Parties became vehicles for elections rather than for year-round mass activity
Voters lost the legal right to join a political party after the franchise widened
options.misconception: invents a legal bar on membership to explain a fall in joining

options.text: Membership was replaced by an official register of party supporters
options.misconception: confuses declining membership with the creation of a state register

options.text: Voters now pick candidates directly and bypass the parties altogether
options.misconception: describes a different electoral arrangement, not a fall in membership

questions.explanation: The decline follows from what parties are actually for. Once a party's main work is nominating candidates, contesting elections and running government, the ordinary member has no task to perform between elections, and a supporter can back a party without joining it. That is why membership fell while competition between parties stayed lively. A legal bar on joining, a state register of supporters, or a world in which candidates are chosen outside any party are three different arrangements, and none is the change described.
questions.hint: Ask what an ordinary member is expected to do once elections become the main business.

questions.learningObjective: identify the trade-off built into a catch-all party
questions.stem: A party advertises itself as a catch-all, appealing across the whole electorate rather than to one social group. What usually changes in how it behaves?

options.text: It widens its appeal and softens the demands made by its committed core
It sets a membership fee that only affluent supporters can realistically meet
options.misconception: pairs a mass-appeal strategy with a rule that narrows membership

options.text: It adopts one demand and refuses to campaign on any other question at all
options.misconception: confuses catch-all breadth with single-issue narrowness

options.text: It requires every member to hold a paid post in the party organisation
options.misconception: invents an occupation requirement to describe a party strategy

questions.explanation: A catch-all party trades ideological sharpness for breadth. To hold voters who disagree with one another, it moves its stated positions toward the middle of the electorate and treats the demands of its committed supporters as negotiable. The strategy only works if something is given up, which is why the same term is used both to describe success and to imply a loss of conviction. A membership fee, a single demand, or a requirement to hold paid office all narrow the appeal instead of widening it.
questions.hint: Ask what a party must give up to keep the support of voters who disagree with each other.

questions.learningObjective: trace how a cartel acts on party competition
questions.stem: A regulator raises the deposit a new party must pay to contest a national election, and afterwards the established parties agree to admit only their own nominees to the list. What is the effect on competition?

options.text: Fewer parties can enter, so competition among the survivors becomes still weaker
More parties can enter, so competition among the new entrants becomes freer
options.misconception: reads a barrier to entry as a widening of the field

options.text: Turnout rises, because paying a deposit makes voters follow the contest closely
options.misconception: confuses a rule about candidates with a rule about voters

options.text: Incumbent parties lose seats, because the deposit is charged to every party alike
options.misconception: assumes incumbents pay the same cost as the parties they exclude

questions.explanation: This is the cartel pattern working through its two instruments. A higher entry deposit narrows the field for the next election, and a closed list stops any new party from appearing at all, so the survivors meet each other less often and can divide the seats among themselves without fear of a breakthrough challenger. The deposit falls on would-be entrants, not on the incumbents drafting the rule, and since almost no voter runs for office, the effect on turnout is a side issue rather than the purpose.
questions.hint: Ask how many parties will be able to compete against each other once both rules are in force.

questions.learningObjective: separate a single-issue party from a green party
questions.stem: A newly registered party campaigns on restricting one named category of resource extraction and refuses to state a position on any other question. What best describes that party?

options.text: A single-issue party, defined by one demand rather than a full programme
A green party, defined by a wide environmental programme across many fields
options.misconception: judges a party by the subject of its issue rather than by the width of its agenda

options.text: A catch-all party, defined by declining to specialise on any question
options.misconception: reads a refusal to specialise as a refusal to have a programme

options.text: A cartel party, defined by bargaining with other parties outside government
options.misconception: mistakes an agreement among parties for a party's own organisational form

questions.explanation: A party that organises itself around one demand and declines to speak on anything else is a single-issue party: the narrowness of the agenda is the defining feature, not the subject of the issue. A green party is defined by a comprehensive environmental programme reaching across many policy areas, so a party like this is not one merely because its demand is ecological. Declining to specialise is the opposite of a catch-all strategy, and negotiating with other parties says nothing at all about how broad or narrow a party's own agenda is.
questions.hint: Ask whether the label is fixed by the subject matter or by the width of the agenda.

questions.learningObjective: identify who fills a party leadership post under a membership ballot
questions.stem: Under one party's rules any member may stand for the leadership, the wider membership votes by ballot, and the winner then leads the party in parliament. Who fills that office?

options.text: The party membership, through a ballot the party is entitled to hold
The parliamentary party alone, in a closed vote with no members present
options.misconception: assumes the wider ballot always happens, ignoring the restricted electorate

options.text: The registered voters of the country, in a separate ballot before the election
options.misconception: confuses an internal party ballot with direct popular selection

options.text: The coalition partners, who must approve the choice to preserve their majority
options.misconception: reads a coalition agreement as authority over an internal party post

If only legislators voted, the choice would rest with a smaller body, which is a different arrangement from the one described rather than the same one. A separate ballot of registered voters would be a second, direct selection outside the party, and a partner's approval belongs to an agreement about forming a government, not to filling an internal post.
questions.hint: Ask which body the rules give the vote to, and how large that body is.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a party congress from a party conference
questions.stem: A party document calls its national congress a delegate meeting of the whole membership, and its conference a smaller meeting of the parliamentary party and officials. Which line does the document draw?

A meeting that settles policy against one that only nominates a candidate
options.misconception: assumes the two bodies are separated by the task they perform

options.text: A meeting held in the capital against one held in a regional city
options.misconception: reads a difference of location as the defining distinction

options.text: A meeting open to the press against one that is always held in private
options.misconception: treats press access as the test for what a party body is

Venue and press access are conventions that vary without changing what the body is, and the document gives no basis for separating one into a policy body and the other into a nominating one.

questions.learningObjective: classify a primary by its electorate and name its effect
questions.stem: A party rule reads that only voters registered with the party before a stated date may vote in its pre-election contest between candidates. What kind of primary does that rule create, and what does it favour?

An open primary, letting any registered party voter influence the result
options.misconception: reads a membership cut-off as an invitation to all party voters

options.text: A closed primary, favouring whichever faction has the fewest members
options.misconception: reverses the turnout advantage that a restricted electorate creates

options.text: An open primary, removing party membership as any influence on the outcome
options.misconception: believes restricting the electorate weakens organised membership

An open primary admits any of the party's registered voters whatever their prior allegiance, so a rule that shuts them out cannot be the open version.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply the distinction between a plurality and a majority
questions.stem: A report states that in an election to a 500-seat chamber the leading party took 240 seats, three short of a majority, and no other party came close to it. Under which rule is that the wrong description?

options.text: A majority rule, because 240 of 500 is short of the 251 seats required
A plurality rule, because a plurality can only be declared below half the seats
options.misconception: believes a plurality requires less than a majority of seats to be valid

options.text: A proportional rule, because seats should match each party's vote share exactly
options.misconception: applies the standard of exact proportionality to a seat count

options.text: A majority rule, because a majority must be settled in a second round
options.misconception: assumes a majority always forces a second round regardless of the result

questions.explanation: A majority is more than half the seats available, which in a 500-seat chamber means 251. With 240 the party leads but has not reached a majority, so the word majority is the wrong description. A plurality rule needs no second round because it settles on the largest single share, and a party holding 240 seats plainly has the largest share under that rule. A proportional rule would return seats roughly in line with each party's votes and would not produce such a solid block, and a second round follows only when a majority is required and not delivered.
questions.hint: Count what share of the chamber 240 seats represents, and compare it with half.

questions.topic: Majoritarian bonus against a broad claim
questions.learningObjective: use the seat-to-vote gap to test a party's breadth claim
questions.stem: A party wins seats across an entire country under a single-member system, finishes with a seat share well above its vote share, and presents itself as the representative of the whole nation. Which feature of the result tells against that claim?

options.text: Its seat bonus, which comes from districts it wins by a narrow margin
Its national coverage, which shows voters chose it in every region
options.misconception: reads broad geographic coverage as evidence of genuine broad support

options.text: Its size, which is far too great to be a vehicle for one group
options.misconception: treats a large seat bloc as proof that no narrow constituency backs it

options.text: Its victory, which shows no other party came near the result
options.misconception: assumes a large margin rules out a seat-to-vote distortion

questions.explanation: A seat share above the vote share is the majoritarian bonus, and it is produced by winning seats on narrow pluralities: a district a party leads by two points returns the same single seat as a district it leads by twenty, and the surplus votes in the second case are simply not converted into further seats. That bonus is exactly what a bloc operating in single-member districts accumulates, and it is paid for by the smaller parties' voters cast elsewhere. Geographic coverage, a large bloc and an outright win are all consistent with the claim rather than evidence against it.
questions.hint: Ask where the extra seats came from, given that each district returns a fixed number.

questions.learningObjective: explain the tactical logic of a two-round system
questions.stem: A country holds a first round in single-member districts and a run-off only where nobody has a majority. A party tells supporters to back its strongest candidate first time, even in districts that candidate leads comfortably. Why?

options.text: To avoid wasting a first-round vote on a candidate who cannot reach a majority
To avoid wasting a seat by splitting the party's vote among too many candidates
options.misconception: applies plurality logic to a rule that decides on a majority

options.text: To avoid an empty ballot box by cutting the number of names on the paper
options.misconception: reduces a tactical choice to a technical rule about ballots

options.text: To avoid a delay by making sure no district ever needs a run-off
options.misconception: believes a party can remove the majority requirement by its own instruction

questions.explanation: Under a two-round rule the winner of a district is the candidate who reaches a majority, so a candidate polling a small share in the first round cannot win that seat and every vote for them is spent. Concentrating the party's support behind the strongest candidate directs it toward districts where the threshold is reachable, which is the whole point of the tactic. The risk the party accepts is that a strong candidate's surplus support in safe districts cannot be transferred, so those voters stay at home or go elsewhere; but the aim is not to save a seat that a plurality would already have delivered.

questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a party leadership selection
questions.stem: A party fills its national leadership through a formal written procedure. Put these four steps in the order that procedure requires, from the first to the last.

The rules for who may stand are fixed and the nomination period closes
Delegates vote and the executive certifies the count before announcing it
The winner takes office and then appoints the remaining party officers

The rules for who may stand have to be settled and the nomination window closed before anyone can be named, because the list of candidates is only valid if it was drawn up under rules that were fixed in advance. Only then do delegates vote, and the executive certifies the tally, because a decision carries authority only once verified. Installation comes last, since no one can be given an office before the body entitled to grant it has decided.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism driving parties toward the centre
questions.stem: Explain why a two-party system tends to push both of its parties toward the middle of the political spectrum.

answer.exemplar: With only two parties, the votes a party can win are the votes its opponent already holds, so the group that decides the seat is the one lying between the two positions offered. Each party therefore gains by moving toward that middle group and loses little by disappointing the committed voters at its own extreme, because those voters have nowhere else to go. The result is reduced ideological distance rather than agreement: the parties still differ, they simply differ less, and the effect is strongest where the two are close. A lawful third party interrupts the squeeze, because a voter's best option is then no longer split between the two.

questions.explanation: A model answer should identify the marginal voter, show that the incentive depends on there being no third option, and say what would break the mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask whose votes are the marginal ones, and what changes if a lawful alternative exists.

questions.learningObjective: explain how a closed primary rewards organised membership
questions.stem: Explain why a closed primary can hand a nomination to the faction with the most members, and say what an open primary would change.

answer.exemplar: A closed primary admits only voters registered with the party before a cut-off, so the electorate is whoever the party has already enrolled rather than whoever is willing to choose between the two candidates. The faction with the largest and most reliable membership can then concentrate that membership at the ballot box, and it has the strongest motive to do so because its members gain from the arrangement they are defending. Opening the primary admits party voters who never registered and those who sympathise with the other faction, which enlarges the electorate beyond the members and removes the enrolment advantage, so a candidate appealing mainly to non-members can now win without first building a party membership.

questions.learningObjective: identify what a single-member district system guarantees

A seat share matching each party's national vote share, within a small margin

options.misconception: reads an optional run-off as something a district rule always requires

questions.learningObjective: separate a confidence-and-supply pact from a coalition
questions.stem: A minority government stays in office because a supporting party backs it on budgets and no-confidence votes but will not sit in the cabinet. What is that arrangement called?

options.text: A confidence-and-supply agreement, sustaining a cabinet from outside
A coalition, in which every supporting party shares the ministerial portfolios
options.misconception: treats external support and shared government as the same thing

options.text: A caretaker government, holding office until the next scheduled election
options.misconception: confuses a voting arrangement with a transitional one

options.text: A single-party system, in which one party holds an unchallengeable majority

Whether the chosen view is the best available is a claim about judgement, not about how many options the electorate sees, and a programme may record every view without any of them reaching the campaign.
questions.hint: Ask how many distinct positions a voter actually hears during the campaign.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: trace how a threshold alters seats and votes
questions.stem: A proportional system ignores every party polling below 5 percent and distributes those votes among the parties that cleared the bar. What follows?

options.text: Small parties lose seats they might have won, and larger parties gain
Small parties keep their seats but forfeit the right to debate policy
options.misconception: invents a speech penalty that the threshold does not impose

options.text: Voters below the bar are reassigned to the nearest district count
options.misconception: describes a transfer of voters rather than of votes

options.text: The seats left vacant are filled by a second round of voting
options.misconception: invents a run-off to explain a rule that simply excludes parties

questions.explanation: A threshold governs the conversion of votes into seats. A party below the bar has no representation at all, and its votes are pooled with the others, so the threshold acts both as a barrier to small parties and as a subsidy to those already above it, which is why it also reduces the number of parties represented. It attaches no penalty to speaking, it does not move any voter to another count, and it does not trigger a second round: excluded parties simply take no seats.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a vote cast for a party that cannot take a seat.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: state the usual rule on substituting a list candidate
questions.stem: Ten days before polling, a candidate on a party's list resigns. The party substitutes a replacement whose name was not printed on the ballot. What follows under the usual rule on substitution?

options.text: The change stands, provided it was made inside the stated time and manner
The change is void, so the seat passes to the party with the next result
options.misconception: assumes a substitution forfeits the seat rather than replacing a name

options.text: The whole list is void, so every other candidate loses their seat
options.misconception: makes one resignation void the independent places of all candidates

options.text: The change stands, but the replacement must also be elected alone
options.misconception: adds a separate election that no substitution rule requires

questions.explanation: A substitution rule exists so that a resignation, a death or a disqualification does not cost a party the seats it won, and it works by allowing a replacement name to be substituted within a prescribed window and by a prescribed procedure. The substitution is not void, and it certainly does not void the rest of the list, since each candidate's place depends on the order of the list rather than on the presence of any one other name. A separate election for the replacement would be a different device requiring its own legal basis.
questions.hint: Ask why a list system would provide for substitution at all.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify what an open primary changes
questions.stem: A party opens its pre-election contest to any registered voter of the state, not only to its own members. What changes most as a result?

options.text: The electorate widens, so winning no longer needs an enrolled membership
The electorate narrows, because non-members are kept out of the contest
options.misconception: describes a restricted electorate while naming it an opening

options.text: Voting becomes compulsory, because every citizen may now take part
options.misconception: turns an eligibility rule into an obligation to vote

options.text: The party's own rules are replaced by the state election code
options.misconception: supposes state law takes over a party's internal nomination

questions.explanation: An open primary admits everyone the state recognises as a voter of that party, including those who never enrolled and those who sympathise with a rival faction, so the winner no longer has to be whoever can turn out the largest enrolled membership. Membership becomes an asset in the contest rather than the condition of entering it, which is why parties that organise well fear the open version. A narrower electorate is the closed case, participation remains voluntary, and a party's internal nomination is not displaced by the code governing the general election.
questions.hint: Ask who may now vote that could not vote before.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: predict how splitting a bloc changes district results
questions.stem: A party's voters sit mainly in two neighbouring districts, where it leads by small margins. A boundary review splits each of those in half between new districts. What is likely to happen?

options.text: The party loses seats, because a split bloc no longer leads anywhere
The party gains seats, because four districts offer four separate chances
options.misconception: counts opportunities without asking who leads in each one

options.text: Its national vote share rises, because each half votes on its own account
options.misconception: invents a change in the national total from a boundary change

options.text: Nothing changes, because a party's total votes fix its total seats
options.misconception: assumes seats follow a national total in a district system

questions.explanation: A party that leads a district by a narrow margin takes the whole seat, and dividing a concentrated bloc across four districts can leave it short of the lead in every one of them. That is why splitting a concentrated bloc is a standard tactic in district systems, and it only works because the count is local and the second place in a district earns nothing. National totals would make boundaries irrelevant, and a boundary cannot create new votes out of the same electorate.
questions.hint: Ask what a single-member district does with a party that comes second in it.

questions.learningObjective: predict the turnout effect of an enrolment requirement
questions.stem: A state requires every voter to enrol in person at one office some distance from where most people live, and offers no alternative arrangement. What is expected?

options.text: Turnout falls, because added travel and time deter some voters
Turnout rises, because citizens value a ceremony held once each cycle
options.misconception: invents a positive effect from an administrative inconvenience

options.text: Turnout is unchanged, because the requirement is identical for everyone
options.misconception: confuses equal treatment with equal effect on willingness

options.text: Turnout doubles, because enrolling fixes the date of the election
options.misconception: claims an enrolment rule sets the election calendar

questions.explanation: An in-person requirement at an inconvenient place adds travel and time to the cost of voting, and turnout falls because that burden is not spread evenly: it bites hardest on the people with least time and least money, so an identical rule still produces unequal participation. A ceremony is not something a state offers to make voting attractive, and an enrolment rule has no bearing on the date polling is held.
questions.hint: Ask what the requirement costs a voter who has to travel, and who bears that cost most.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: compute which parties can take seats under a threshold
questions.stem: A 200-seat proportional chamber has a 5 percent threshold. Three parties win 48, 30 and 6 percent of the vote, and two more win 4 percent each. How many of the 200 seats can the two 4 percent parties obtain?

options.text: None, because each is below the bar and its votes go to the others
Sixteen, because 4 percent of 200 is about eight seats apiece
options.misconception: multiplies a vote share into seats while ignoring the threshold

options.text: Eight, because the threshold excludes only the smaller of the two
options.misconception: invents a rule that treats equal shares differently

options.text: Two hundred, because a proportional rule allocates every vote cast
options.misconception: ignores that the rule does not count votes below the bar

questions.explanation: The threshold is checked before any allocation happens, and both 4 percent parties fall short of 5 percent, so neither can take a seat. Their combined 8 percent of votes is instead distributed among the parties that qualified, which is why the qualified parties end up with slightly more than their own shares. Multiplying 4 percent by 200 gives a notional figure of eight seats, but a notional share is not an entitlement, because the threshold is precisely the rule that says such a share is not converted into seats. A proportional rule allocates the votes it counts, and it does not count these.
questions.hint: Check the bar before doing any multiplication.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: test a proportionality claim against a threshold rule
questions.stem: A legislature is described as giving every party that won votes a seat share matching its vote share, and its rule sets a 5 percent threshold below which no seats are allocated. What tells against the description?

options.text: A party below the bar can win votes and take no seat at all
The bar is only 5 percent, so almost no party falls below it
options.misconception: treats a low threshold as though it excluded nobody

options.text: Seats are allocated by a commission, so no formula is really used
options.misconception: replaces the claim with a complaint about who administers the rule

options.text: Turnout is published, so the vote shares cannot be compared
options.misconception: invents a secrecy problem out of published turnout figures

questions.explanation: The description promises a match between votes and seats for every party that won votes, and a threshold creates a class of parties that win votes and receive nothing, so the promise does not hold for them however reasonable the bar looks. A threshold of 5 percent still excludes somebody in every election, so its modest size does not rescue the claim. Who administers the allocation and whether turnout is published are facts about transparency rather than about whether votes and seats correspond.
questions.hint: Ask whether the promise covers a party that won votes but fell below the bar.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: test a spending and vote result against a resource explanation
questions.stem: A commission reports that in a typical district the sitting member spent three times as much as each challenger, and the member's share of the vote rose compared with the previous contest. Which reading fits both figures?

options.text: The extra spending bought recognition, and recognition helps a candidate
The extra spending proves the member's policies were better received
options.misconception: reads a correlation as proof about the content of a policy

options.text: The higher vote share shows the district was redrawn in the member's favour
options.misconception: infers a boundary change from a change in votes alone

options.text: The spending gap shows challengers were legally barred from spending
options.misconception: turns a difference in outlay into a prohibition

questions.explanation: Spending in a constituency buys advertising and visibility, and visibility is one of the better established predictors of a vote, so the pair of figures is consistent with a resource explanation without needing to claim anything about the merit of a policy. The same two figures cannot establish that a boundary was redrawn, since a changed vote share is exactly what a competent campaign would produce on unchanged boundaries, and a difference in outlay is not a legal bar on anyone. The explanation has to fit both numbers without adding facts the report does not contain.
questions.hint: Ask what one spending figure and one vote figure can support together.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: trace the bargaining pressure created by a majority requirement
questions.stem: A country elects its president in two rounds. The first is inconclusive, and the two leaders are rivals each backed by a separate coalition. Which consequence does the design make harder to avoid?

options.text: Negotiation with the runner-up, because a majority needs second preferences
A single decisive night, because the rule removes any need to compromise
options.misconception: believes a run-off settles a contest without any bargaining

options.text: The defeat of both coalitions, since neither can claim a popular mandate
options.misconception: infers that a run-off dissolves the coalitions behind the candidates

options.text: A repeat of the first round, because the rule allows one ballot only
options.misconception: invents a third ballot from a rule that provides two

questions.explanation: A majority requirement means nobody can win outright on first preferences, so anyone seeking a broad mandate has to obtain support from the other side's voters, and the incentive to court those preferences is built into the counting rule rather than left to taste. The second round also gives the runner-up something concrete to trade, which is why coalition partners have an interest in how their leader negotiates. The design extends rather than removes the need to bargain, it does not dissolve either coalition, and the second round happens once per contest rather than being repeated.
questions.hint: Ask what a candidate must still be missing after the first ballot.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: compare the seat effects of two allocation rules
questions.stem: Two systems each claim to give voters the strongest possible say. In one a party on 30 percent of the vote can hold a legislative majority; in the other it cannot. Where does the difference come from?

options.text: From district rules that over-reward the leading party in each seat
From the fact that the largest party always wins more votes than rivals
options.misconception: credits an out-reward effect to the size of the vote lead

options.text: From the proportional rule, which ignores districts entirely by design
options.misconception: claims a proportional rule discards constituency information

options.text: From a rule that stops any party from holding half the seats alone
options.misconception: invents a bar on majorities that the two systems do not share

questions.explanation: A single-member district turns a narrow plurality into a whole seat, so a party leading most districts by small margins takes a legislative majority on well under half of the national vote; that is the majoritarian bias, and it is the source of the difference the two claims describe. In a proportional system the vote-to-seat ratio is the same for every party, so 30 percent of votes yields about 30 percent of seats and a majority requires approaching half the vote. A proportional rule does not discard constituency information, and no rule prevents a party from holding half the seats.
questions.hint: Ask what a single district does with the votes of the candidate who comes second.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a campaign from nomination to poll
questions.stem: A regulated general election follows its own fixed timetable. Put these four steps in the order the timetable requires, from the first to the last.

options.text: The party settles which candidate it will field in that constituency
The campaign opens and the candidate sets out the party's platform
Broadcast time and printed space are allocated under the agreed rules
Polling takes place and the returning officer certifies the count

questions.explanation: The timetable is ordered by dependency. A candidate has to exist before the campaign can speak, since it is the candidate who states the platform and answers for it. The campaign then runs, and the rules allocating airtime and printed space are fixed in advance so that access is settled by regulation rather than by negotiation between rivals, which is what stops the contest becoming a bidding war for exposure. Polling comes last of all, and the count cannot be certified until after the ballots have been cast.
questions.hint: Ask what must be settled before the campaign can say anything at all.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of coalition bargaining
questions.stem: No party has won a majority and several are willing to govern. Put these four steps in the order the bargaining requires, from the first to the last.

options.text: The largest party establishes that it cannot govern on its own numbers
It approaches each possible partner separately about what it wants
The partners settle a set of policies they will each be held to
The agreement is signed and the portfolios are divided among the signatories

questions.explanation: Bargaining cannot start before it is established that partners are needed, because an approach made by a party that can govern alone carries no weight. The approaches then have to be made separately, since a set of demands put to all possible partners at once is a set of demands that each of them can wait to see the others concede. Only once there are private understandings can the partners settle the policies they will be held to, and the division of portfolios follows from the bargain they have struck.
questions.hint: Ask what a party must know before its demands carry any weight.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain why requests are reconciled before legislative debate
questions.stem: A legislature will not consider spending until the executive has turned departmental requests into one bill with a settled total. Why finish that step before members are involved?

options.text: So departmental demands are reconciled against revenue before debate begins
So the legislature can add new spending items during its own hearings
options.misconception: mistakes a legislature's amending power for the purpose of drafting

options.text: So the executive can be certain the bill will pass without a vote
options.misconception: supposes an executive controls the outcome of a legislative vote

options.text: So departments need not state their spending requests in writing
options.misconception: reverses the point of collecting written submissions

questions.explanation: The finance bill is the point at which competing claims on a fixed revenue are reconciled. Departments ask for what they need, and the ministry has to fit those requests inside a settled total, so by the time members are asked to debate they are looking at one coherent set of totals rather than a list of departmental wishes never tested against the money available. Amending a bill in committee is a power the legislature holds afterwards, not the reason for the drafting step, and an executive can never be sure of a vote, which is exactly why the reconciliation has to happen first.
questions.hint: Ask what a single settled total does to the separate demands that go into it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: select the consequences of an electoral threshold
questions.stem: A proportional system applies a threshold and redistributes the votes of parties that fail to reach it. Which of the following follow from that rule? Select all that apply.

options.text: Parties below the bar are stopped from converting votes into seats
The votes of excluded parties are shared out among the qualified ones
The number of parties able to expect seats is larger than without a bar
options.misconception: assumes a filter widens the field of parties reaching a chamber

options.text: A party's own vote total becomes a weaker guide to its seat total
An excluded party must contest a primary before standing again
options.misconception: invents an internal consequence no seat rule imposes

questions.explanation: A threshold acts at three connected points. It blocks the excluded party from taking any seat, it sends that party's votes into the pool shared with the parties that qualified, and it therefore makes a party's own vote total a less reliable guide to its seat total, since two parties with the same votes can end up with very different seats. The number of parties reaching the chamber goes down rather than up, because the rule is a filter, and nothing in it touches how a party chooses its candidate.
questions.hint: Ask, for each claim, whether the redistribution rule actually produces it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: compute a party's seat total from vote shares
questions.stem: A 300-seat chamber is elected proportionally. Three parties won 40, 35 and 25 percent of the vote, with no threshold in force. How many seats does the 25 percent party take?

options.text: Seventy-five, because 25 percent of 300 is 75
One hundred, because 300 seats are divided among three parties equally
options.misconception: divides seats equally instead of in proportion to votes

options.text: A hundred and five, because the party is entitled to a seat bonus
options.misconception: invents a bonus rule that no proportional system contains

options.text: Nothing, because a party needs a majority of votes to take any seat
options.misconception: mistakes a majority of seats for a majority of the vote

questions.explanation: With no threshold in force, proportionality means the seats-per-vote ratio is the same for every party, so 25 percent of 300 seats is exactly 75. The shares add to 100 percent here, so no rounding is needed and the other two parties take 120 and 105. Dividing 300 equally among three parties would require all three to have polled identically, and a proportional rule contains no bonus for large parties. Nor does a party need a majority of votes to take seats; a majority of seats needs close to a majority of votes.
questions.hint: Multiply the party's vote share by the size of the chamber.
